content:
Back in May, as part of an ICERM workshop, a group of us developed the theory of Riemann integration and Riemann-Stieltjes integration, where the integrand and integrator were allowed to be vector-valued. Part of the rationale for doing this was that at the time, the API for signed measures was not in place in Mathlib, so we could not use the Lebesgue (measure-theoretic) approach to integration and opted instead for the more classical Riemann approach (based on convergence of Riemann sums or Riemann-Stieltjes sums). However, the theory of vector valued measures has now been substantially developed in Mathlib, to the point where most of the applications we had in mind for the Riemann-Stieltjes integral can now be done using vector-valued Lebesgue integration instead. So it seems unlikely that our full code will end up in Mathlib in the end.

This is fine, but I am wondering longer-term what is the plan for how Mathlib will handle concepts, such as Riemann integration, which are weaker than another standard concept (in this case, Lebesgue integration, which can handle all the Riemann integrable functions and more besides), but are still of mathematical interest. As a concrete example, consider for instance Lebesgue's theorem that a function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable if and only if it is bounded and almost everywhere continuous. At present, there is no idiomatic way to even state this theorem using Mathlib definitions, because the Riemann integral is only defined implicitly (one can tease it out of the BoxIntegral API, but not in a particularly discoverable fashion). On the other hand, if one develops too extensive an API for the Riemann integral, this may cause some users to use that integral over the more powerful Lebesgue integral, necessitating some additional conversions between the two integrals when trying to merge together different proofs that use different notions of integration.

I wonder if there is some sort of compromise position in which Mathlib can at least provide a idiomatic definition of such weak, but standardized and mainstream mathematical concepts (such as the Riemann integral), but provide guidance in docstrings that use of a stronger notion (in this case, the Lebesgue integral) is strongly preferred unless the application specifically requires the weak notion only? This would allow Mathlib to provide a basic level of support to the (small) portion of math devoted to these weaker concepts, without losing the benefits of having a coherent API centered around the strong version.

Terence Tao said:

I wonder if there is some sort of compromise position in which Mathlib can at least provide a idiomatic definition of such weak, but standardized and mainstream mathematical concepts (such as the Riemann integral), but provide guidance in docstrings that use of a stronger notion (in this case, the Lebesgue integral) is strongly preferred unless the application specifically requires the weak notion only? This would allow Mathlib to provide a basic level of support to the (small) portion of math devoted to these weaker concepts, without losing the benefits of having a coherent API centered around the strong version.

I have the impression that the design of Mathlib is geared toward forward development of mathematics (include the most general environment to support mathematical project X), and not geared so much toward reverse (or introspective) development (find the smallest set of Mathlib which represents the weakest set of axioms from which one can develop the strongest theory). This latter part is especially important for the development of reverse mathematics, but it is also useful in determining simpler alternatives to develop a mathematical theory.

I would like to see a Mathlib User's Guide (perhaps there is one already) which talks about how to use Mathlib in various contexts. Terry's example above (Riemann instead of Lebesgue integration) and my current project (refactoring Sylvester-Schur) are two cases where Mathlib at present is geared toward using the strongest results available instead of something less general and more targeted. It may be that the answer for these kinds of projects is not to use Mathlib, but identify those portions of Mathlib that are included, and then "dup" those parts and adjust or weaken them for the project at hand. The Mathlib library now becomes a template, not just a library, for creating new library fragments, and that math[s] projects should include not just which portions of Mathlib were used directly, but also which were used indirectly and how they were modified to satisfy the demands of the given project.

Nice as it would be to have a "super-repository" of these modifications, it might be enough to have a user's guide and a database of how such modifications were used, so that later researchers could use the database to garner the intent of the fragment and then make their own version of the fragment for further use.

Yaël Dillies said:

Your Mathlib User Guide is basically leanprover-community/mathlib-phrasebook

I am looking forward to the phrasebook. However (to extend the analogy), I need to make an effective sales pitch, so I need a cultural guide or sales guide, not just a set of phrases. Moving away from the analogy, I want to see community-approved examples of other projects where the goal was met not by referring to Mathlib purely, but by building an appropriate library fragment and then using that fragment to meet the goal. This would be community approved not just because of the main theorems/APIs developed by the fragment, but also because of the process used in fragment-making, which process and products might direct the development of Mathlib itself. If it indeed resembles a phrasebook, I think my idea of User Guide is not met by a Mathlib phrasebook. I'll check out the phrasebook anyway in case I'm wrong about it.

content:
what to do with weak but standard math. Does the phrasebook answer this?

It could: the chapter on integration could mention "mathlib does not use the Riemann integral, but the Lebesgue integral instead"; the chapter on linear algebra could mention "mathlib does not have VectorSpace k E --- but Module k E is the same thing", etc.
(There is care to be taken to not turn the phrasebook into a reference, but that can be solved. If necessary by only briefly mentioning this and pointing to e.g. #mil for longer explanations.)

There is also section 15.9 suggesting one makes ones own definition of Variety; this is the closest I have seen in the phrasebook to the current topic. I am talking about something slightly larger in scope. Perhaps an illuminating example would be near-rings or asymptotic/almost substructures of groups or rings. Presuming these subjects have not made their way into Mathlib, what would be a good way of developing them based on the patterns in Mathlib, without calling on the Mathlib lemmata directly?

content: To get back to the question, what would people feel about a Riemann integral directory in mathlib with module docstrings saying "don't develop API for this, use the lesbesgue integral, here are a few theorems"? The fact that we can't even state a result which we might explain to the undergraduates without the definition seems to me to be an argument for the inclusion of the Riemann integral in mathlib.

Another option is to put it in Archive: in this way it is easy to give pointers, it evolves with Mathlib, but there is no possibility to overuse it. And if one day it turns out that one of the results there is useful for an application, then it's easy to move it back to the main Mathlib.
For specifically Riemann integration I think we already have that with docs#BoxIntegral.integral.

Just for reference, here is what the Riemann integral would look like when defined directly from BoxIntegral:

import Mathlib

open BoxIntegral

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedSpace ℝ E]

variable (a b : ℝ) (f : ℝ → E) (L : E)

def HasRiemannIntegral' (h : a < b) : Prop := HasIntegral
    ⟨fun (_ : Fin 1) ↦ a, fun _ ↦ b, fun _ ↦ by grind⟩
    IntegrationParams.Riemann
    (f <| · 0) BoxAdditiveMap.volume L

def HasRiemannIntegral : Prop :=
  if heq : a = b then L = 0 else
    if h : a < b then HasRiemannIntegral' a b f L h else
      HasRiemannIntegral' b a f (-L) (by order)

def RiemannIntegrable : Prop := ∃ L, HasRiemannIntegral a b f L

open Classical in
noncomputable def riemannIntegral : E :=
  if h : RiemannIntegrable a b f then h.choose else 0

notation3 "∫ʳ "(...)" in "a".."b", "r:60:(scoped f => f) => riemannIntegral a b r
I have created a new PR #41596 to commit the Riemann/Riemann-Stieltjes integral definitions to Archive.
